correct_citation: Morrow-Howell, N., Jonson-Reid, M., McCrary, S., Lee, Y., & Spitznagel, E. (2009). Evaluation of Experience Corps: Student reading outcomes (CSD Research Report 09-01). St. Louis: Washington University, Center for Social Development. Reviewed in WWC Quick Review, February 2010.
design: Randomized controlled trial (two-group pre-post with random assignment); WWC: well-implemented RCT consistent with evidence standards
population_location: 883 pretested (825 at posttest) at-risk grade 1-3 students in 23 schools in Boston, New York City and Port Arthur, TX
outcome: Passage comprehension (standardized test) and teacher-rated grade-specific reading skills; also receptive vocabulary and phonemic awareness (no significant effects)
effect_as_reported: ES 0.13 (passage comprehension) and 0.16 (teacher-assessed reading skills); among students with at least 35 sessions, effects stronger, ES .13 to .17
excerpt: Students in the Experience Corps program made greater gains over the academic year on passage comprehension and on general reading skills as assessed by their teachers, with effect sizes of 0.13 and 0.16, respectively.
note: WWC says "Nearly 900" students; the 883 figure and the 35-session dose result come from the original report ("When including only the EC students who received at least 35 sessions ... the effects were stronger"). Effects smaller for special education students.

correct_citation: Black, A. R., Somers, M.-A., Doolittle, F., Unterman, R., & Grossman, J. B. (2009). The Evaluation of Enhanced Academic Instruction in After-School Programs: Final Report (NCEE 2009-4077). Washington, DC: NCEE, Institute of Education Sciences.
design: Randomized trial (students randomly assigned within after-school centers to enhanced or regular program); two-year offer is intent-to-treat
population_location: Grade 2-5 students in 21st CCLC after-school centers; this report covers 27 centers (12 reading) in both years, US
outcome: SAT 10 total reading score (also vocabulary, reading comprehension, word study subtests; DIBELS fluency)
effect_as_reported: One year: no statistically significant impact on SAT 10 total reading. Two-year offer: -5.6 scaled score points (effect size -0.17 SD, p = 0.04); comprehension and vocabulary subtests -7.6 points each
excerpt: However, for reading there were no positive effects on achievement after one year of the program, and findings after two years indicated the enhanced reading program led to slower progress in reading than did the regular after-school programming.
note: Headline outcome is SAT 10 total reading, not comprehension alone, though the comprehension subtest was also negative at two years. The regular-program group got "a mix of homework help and other services not focused on reading" (17% and 12% got some reading instruction), not homework help alone.

correct_citation: Bowen, D. H., & Kisida, B. (2023). Investigating the causal effects of arts education. Journal of Policy Analysis and Management, 42(3), 624-647. doi:10.1002/pam.22449 (online 2022; earlier HERC report 2019).
design: Randomized controlled trial (school-level lottery of arts partnerships)
population_location: 42 elementary and middle schools in Houston, Texas (Houston ISD); 15,886 students in grades 3-8 in the assigned sample
outcome: Standardized math, reading and science achievement (null); writing achievement, disciplinary infractions, emotional empathy (positive)
effect_as_reported: No effects on math, reading, or science achievement (no point estimate given in this sentence)
excerpt: Though we find no effects on math, reading, or science achievement, the positive effects on writing achievement are particularly noteworthy.
note: Journal title is "Investigating the Causal Effects of Arts Education"; the "Experimental Evidence from Houston's Arts Access Initiative" title belongs to the 2019 HERC report. JPAM print issue is 2023 vol. 42(3).

correct_citation: Durkin, K., Lipsey, M. W., Farran, D. C., & Wiesen, S. E. (2022). Effects of a statewide prekindergarten program on children's achievement and behavior through sixth grade. Developmental Psychology, 58(3), 470-484. doi:10.1037/dev0001301
design: Randomized controlled trial (oversubscribed sites; random offer of admission vs wait-list control), longitudinal
population_location: 2,990 children from low-income families who applied to Tennessee Voluntary Pre-K (TN-VPK) sites statewide, Tennessee
outcome: State achievement tests (TCAP grade 3; TNReady grade 6) in reading/ELA, math and science; also discipline, attendance, special education
effect_as_reported: Grade 6 ITT effect sizes: ELA -0.128, math -0.178, science -0.132 SD (all p < .05); TOT about -0.24 to -0.33 SD. Grade 3 reading difference not significant in unweighted analysis
excerpt: On the 6th grade TNReady tests, control children continued to outperform the TN-VPK children in reading, mathematics, and science with statistically significant differences larger than those observed in 3rd grade.
note: Supported for grade 6. In grade 3, differences were significant for math and science only (unweighted) and for all three in weighted analyses.

correct_citation: Cipriano, C., Strambler, M. J., Naples, L. H., Ha, C., Kirk, M., Wood, M., Sehgal, K., Zieher, A. K., Eveleigh, A., McCarthy, M., Funaro, M., Ponnock, A., Chow, J. C., & Durlak, J. (2023). The state of evidence for social and emotional learning: A contemporary meta-analysis of universal school-based SEL interventions. Child Development, 94(5), 1181-1204. doi:10.1111/cdev.13968
design: Systematic review and meta-analysis (424 studies, 2008-2020)
population_location: 575,361 K-12 students in 53 countries; 252 discrete universal school-based SEL interventions
outcome: Skills, attitudes, behaviors, school climate and safety, peer relationships, school functioning, academic achievement
effect_as_reported: Significant improvement in academic achievement versus controls; pooled effect size not in fetched abstract (Wiley full text returned 403)
excerpt: compared to control conditions, students who participate in USB SEL interventions experienced significantly improved skills, attitudes, behaviors, school climate and safety, peer relationships, school functioning, and academic achievement.
note: Title retrieved (see citation). Heterogeneity by content, features, context and implementation quality confirmed in abstract. Pooled achievement g still not retrieved.

correct_citation: Walton, G. M., & Cohen, G. L. (2011). A brief social-belonging intervention improves academic and health outcomes of minority students. Science, 331(6023), 1447-1451. doi:10.1126/science.1198364
design: Randomized controlled trial (WWC: RCT with low attrition, meets standards without reservations)
population_location: 92 college freshmen (49 African American, 43 European American) at a selective US university
outcome: Cumulative GPA sophomore to senior year; self-reported health and doctor visits
effect_as_reported: Raised African Americans' GPA and halved the minority achievement gap; WWC: Black students 3.60 vs 3.34 GPA, improvement index 24 (37 students); full sample 3.57 vs 3.48, not significant
excerpt: over the 3-year observation period the intervention raised African Americans' grade-point average (GPA) relative to multiple control groups and halved the minority achievement gap.
note: WWC page: "Meets WWC standards without reservations because it is a randomized controlled trial with low attrition." WWC analytic sample is 70 students (37 Black), not 92. The WWC page misprints the second author as "Cohen, C. L."

correct_citation: Balfanz, R., & Byrnes, V. (2013). Meeting the Challenge of Combating Chronic Absenteeism: Impact of the NYC Mayor's Interagency Task Force on Chronic Absenteeism and School Attendance and Its Implications for Other Cities. Everyone Graduates Center, Johns Hopkins University. Also Balfanz, R., & Byrnes, V. (2018). Using data and the human touch: Evaluating the NYC inter-agency campaign to reduce chronic absenteeism. Journal of Education for Students Placed at Risk.
design: Quasi-experimental comparison of 100 task force (pilot) schools with 46 comparison schools; student-level statistical models
population_location: New York City public schools with above-average chronic absenteeism, 2010-2013
outcome: Days attended; chronic absenteeism; high school persistence (remaining in school the following year)
effect_as_reported: Previously chronically absent mentored students gained almost two weeks (9 days) per student per year; mentored high school students 52% more likely to remain in school the following year
excerpt: Previously chronically absent students who had mentors gained almost two additional weeks (9 days) of school per student, per year.
note: 52% quote: "Previously chronically absent high school students with Success Mentors were 52% more likely to remain in school the following year than equivalent comparison students who did not receive mentors". Sample size differs by source: the 2013 report says 100 schools with over 60,000 (or 62,815) students, and 87,685 including comparison schools. The 2018 JESPAR abstract says "100 schools, with over 80,000 students". The JHU Hub page returned 403.

correct_citation: Allen, J. P., Philliber, S., Herrling, S., & Kuperminc, G. P. (1997). Preventing teen pregnancy and academic failure: Experimental evaluation of a developmentally based approach. Child Development, 68(4), 729-742.
design: Randomized controlled trial (random assignment to Teen Outreach or control)
population_location: 695 high school students at 25 sites nationwide, US (1991-1995)
outcome: Course failure, academic suspension, pregnancy at program exit (9 months after entry)
effect_as_reported: Course failure 26.6% (TOP) vs 46.8% (control), statistically significant; lower suspension and pregnancy rates
excerpt: Allen and colleagues (1997) found that youth in the TOP® treatment group had lower levels of course failures (26.6 percent), compared with comparison youth (46.8 percent), at the program exit posttest.
note: The percentages come from CrimeSolutions. The OJP abstract confirms 695 students, 25 sites, random assignment and lower pregnancy, failure and suspension "at exit". Page numbers 729-742 are from memory and were not fetched.

correct_citation: Bergman, P., & Chan, E. W. (2021). Leveraging parents through low-cost technology: The impact of high-frequency information on student achievement. Journal of Human Resources, 56(1), 125-158. doi:10.3368/jhr.56.1.1118-9837R1
design: Randomized controlled trial (grade levels within schools randomly assigned; intent-to-treat)
population_location: Parents of 1,137 students in 22 middle and high schools, Kanawha County Schools, West Virginia (2015-16)
outcome: Course failures, class attendance, retention, state test scores
effect_as_reported: Course failures -27% (published JHR abstract; online appendix June 2019 says 28%); class attendance +12%; retention up; no impact on state test scores
excerpt: The alerts reduced course failures by 27 percent, increased class attendance by 12 percent, and increased student retention, though there was no impact on state test scores.
note: The 27 vs 28% gap is between the published abstract (27) and the online appendix (28); J-PAL also says 27. The listed NBER URL w28581 is a different paper: Berlinski, Busso, Dinkelman & Martinez (Chile text messages). Randomization was by grade within school, not by parent.

correct_citation: Vasilopoulos, F., Jeffrey, H., Wu, Y., & Dumontheil, I. (2023). Multi-level meta-analysis of physical activity interventions during childhood: Effects of physical activity on cognition and academic achievement. Educational Psychology Review, 35, Article 59. doi:10.1007/s10648-023-09760-2
design: Three-level meta-analysis of 92 randomized controlled trials
population_location: Typically developing children aged 5-12 (N = 25,334), multiple countries
outcome: Academic achievement (combined), executive function, on-task behaviour, creativity, fluid intelligence, working memory
effect_as_reported: Academic achievement g = 0.14, p = 0.14, 95% CI -0.04 to 0.31 (moderate-certainty evidence), not significant
excerpt: three-level meta-analysis indicated that PA interventions did not benefit executive function measures (g = 0.09, p = 0.24 (95% CI: − 0.06–0.25), very low-certainty evidence) or academic achievement (g = 0.14, p = 0.14 (95% CI: − 0.04–0.31),
note: Authors retrieved via Crossref and the Birkbeck repository copy; Springer returned a JavaScript challenge. Moderator analyses found math benefits for PA with academic instruction lasting 6-10 weeks.

correct_citation: University of Chicago Crime Lab. Becoming a Man (BAM) [project page]. https://crimelab.uchicago.edu/projects/becoming-a-man-bam/ (accessed 2026-10-18)
design: Project summary of four randomized controlled trials
population_location: Male youth in Chicago public schools
outcome: Student outcomes (later two RCTs); pooled: violent-crime arrests, school engagement
effect_as_reported: Later two studies: no statistically significant effect detected. Pooled four RCTs: violent crime reduced up to 37%, school engagement +0.03 to 0.08 SD
excerpt: we were unable to detect a statistically significant effect of the program on student outcomes as the program expanded to serve different student populations in different school and neighborhood contexts.
note: The page adds that "These results do not affect our overall conclusions when we look at all four studies together".

correct_citation: Bartfeld, J. S., Berger, L., & Men, F. (2020). Universal access to free school meals through the Community Eligibility Provision is associated with better attendance for low-income elementary school students in Wisconsin. Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, 120(2), 210-218. doi:10.1016/j.jand.2019.07.022 (epub 2019 Oct 14)
design: Quasi-experimental difference-in-differences with student fixed effects (1 baseline, 2 follow-up years)
population_location: Wisconsin elementary students grades 1-5; 92,126 observation-years in 37 CEP and 108 eligible non-CEP schools, 2013-14 to 2015-16
outcome: Attendance rate; low attendance (attending fewer than 95% of days)
effect_as_reported: Year 1: no association. Year 2: -3.5 percentage points in share of students with low attendance (P = 0.045); association only for economically disadvantaged students
excerpt: Implementing the CEP had no association with attendance in the initial year. The second year of CEP was associated with a 3.5 percentage point reduction in the percentage of students with low attendance (P=0.045).
note: Year: published in print February 2020, online October 2019. ScienceDirect returned 403, so PubMed was used.

correct_citation: Oster, E., & Thornton, R. (2011). Menstruation, sanitary products, and school attendance: Evidence from a randomized evaluation. American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, 3(1), 91-100. doi:10.1257/app.3.1.91
design: Randomized evaluation (random provision of sanitary products)
population_location: Girls in Nepal
outcome: School attendance during menstruation
effect_as_reported: Menstruation costs about 0.4 days in a 180-day year; sanitary products had no effect on this gap (claim that products close the gap rejected at 1% level)
excerpt: Girls who randomly received sanitary products were no less likely to miss school during their period.

correct_citation: Brunner, E. J., Dougherty, S. M., & Ross, S. L. (2023). The effects of career and technical education: Evidence from the Connecticut Technical High School System. Review of Economics and Statistics, 105(4), 867-882. doi:10.1162/rest_a_01098 (NBER WP 28790, 2021)
design: Regression discontinuity design at estimated school-specific admission score thresholds (fuzzy RD estimating effect of attending)
population_location: Applicants to the 16 stand-alone Connecticut Technical High School System schools, Connecticut
outcome: High school graduation, college enrollment, quarterly earnings, attendance, test scores
effect_as_reported: Males: +10 percentage points high school graduation; +32% quarterly earnings; higher attendance (+1.7 pp) and test scores; little effect for females
excerpt: Male students are 10 percentage points more likely to graduate from high school and have half a semester less time enrolled in college, although effects on college fade-out. Male students have 32% higher quarterly earnings.
note: The paper frames these as effects of attending a technical high school, identified at the admission threshold, not effects of admission itself. REStat details come from Crossref metadata. The UConn 2019-13 working paper was downloaded but not used for the excerpt.

correct_citation: Research for Action / Philadelphia Education Research Consortium (2022). What keeps high school students on track to graduation in the School District of Philadelphia? Also Wills, T., Park, J. E., & Lesnick, J. (2019). On-Track but Vulnerable: 9th Grade Warning Signs of 10th Grade Struggles. School District of Philadelphia Issue Brief.
design: Descriptive longitudinal cohort analyses (correlational)
population_location: First-time ninth graders, School District of Philadelphia
outcome: Four-year graduation rate by ninth-grade on-track status
effect_as_reported: 82% on-track vs 56% off-track (about 26 percentage points; RFA); 87.8-89.2% vs 43.3-48.8% for 2011-12 to 2013-14 cohorts (SDP brief)
excerpt: we saw a graduation rate of 82% for on-track ninth graders, but only 56% for off-track ninth graders, a considerable difference of about 26 percentage points.
note: SDP brief excerpt: "four-year graduation rates were much higher for On-Track students (87.8-89.2%) than for Off-Track students (43.3-48.8%)". The William Penn Foundation report was fetched but not needed for these figures. The two sources cover different cohorts.

correct_citation: Kraft, M. A., & Rogers, T. (2015). The underutilized potential of teacher-to-parent communication: Evidence from a field experiment. Economics of Education Review, 47, 49-63. doi:10.1016/j.econedurev.2015.04.001
design: Randomized field experiment
population_location: High school students in a summer credit-recovery program (US urban district; district not named in fetched text)
outcome: Failure to earn course credit
effect_as_reported: Share failing to earn credit fell from 15.8% to 9.3% (41% reduction), mainly by preventing dropouts
excerpt: Messages decreased the percentage of students who failed to earn course credit from 15.8% to 9.3%—a 41% reduction. This reduction resulted primarily from preventing drop-outs, rather than from reducing failure or dismissal rates.
note: The listed Annenberg URL is dead ("This page doesn't exist"), so the HKS abstract page was used. The "summer" detail comes from Kraft's Boston Fed article ("during a high school summer credit-recovery program").

correct_citation: Magnuson, K. (2003). The effect of increases in welfare mothers' education on their young children's academic and behavioral outcomes: Evidence from the National Evaluation of Welfare-to-Work Strategies Child Outcomes Study (IRP Discussion Paper 1274-03). Madison: Institute for Research on Poverty, University of Wisconsin.
design: Instrumental-variables analysis using random assignment to education-focused (HCD), work-focused (LFA) or control groups in NEWWS
population_location: Welfare-recipient mothers with young children in Atlanta GA, Grand Rapids MI and Riverside CA (NEWWS Child Outcomes Study)
outcome: Children's academic school readiness (Bracken), mother-reported academic problems, behavior
effect_as_reported: 8 months of maternal educational activity: +0.21 SD school readiness, -0.20 SD academic problems; little to no effect on behavior. Readiness effect concentrated among mothers in need of basic education (+.34 Bracken points per month, p < .10)
excerpt: Findings suggest that increases in maternal education are positively associated with children’s academic school readiness, and negatively associated with mothers’ reports of their children’s academic problems, but with little to no effect on children’s behavior.
note: The treatment variable is months in any educational activity (high school/GED, ABE, ESL, vocational training, college), not Adult Basic Education alone; ABE was the most common type. "Low-skilled" matches only the in-need-of-basic-education subgroup, where the readiness effect was marginal (p < .10). The academic-problems effect was not concentrated in that subgroup.

correct_citation: Duffy, M., & Turner, A. (2018, October). The Philadelphia Community Schools Initiative: Year 1 Evaluation. Philadelphia: Research for Action.
design: Implementation evaluation (surveys, interviews, focus groups, document review); no impact estimate
population_location: Philadelphia Community Schools Initiative schools, 2017-18 school year
outcome: Implementation conditions and early short-term outcomes (alignment, partner satisfaction); measurement and evaluation practices
effect_as_reported: No impact estimate
excerpt: Without specific measures, outcomes data have not been collected to date, although individual schools and MOE’s central office tracked attendance rates
note: The report says "Community schools specified broad outcomes but lacked measures to track progress": schools did name outcomes in logic models, but only broad ones. "Did not have specific outcomes in mind" is WHYY's paraphrase, and attendance was tracked. "No impact estimate" is correct.

correct_citation: Bowen, D. H., & Kisida, B. (2021). The Arts Advantage: Impacts of Arts Education on Boston Students. Boston: EdVestors.
design: Quasi-experimental longitudinal analysis; regression with student, grade, school and year fixed effects (timing of arts course enrollment)
population_location: 616,273 K-12 student-level observations in 171 traditional Boston Public Schools, 2008-09 to 2018-19 (eleven school years)
outcome: Attendance (also discipline, ELA and math test scores)
effect_as_reported: Arts course enrollment: attendance +0.2 percent (about one-third of a day per 180-day year); students with IEPs +0.7 day; previously chronically absent students +1.1 days per year
excerpt: We find that when students are enrolled in arts courses, their attendance modestly improves by 0.2 percent, or roughly one-third of a day in a standard 180-day school year.
note: Size now retrieved (see effect). The treatment is enrollment in an arts course in a given year, not a dose of course-taking. "All Boston Public Schools" is precisely 171 traditional public schools. Small middle-school ELA and math gains (0.03, 0.01) were also reported.

correct_citation: Mahoney, J. L., & Cairns, R. B. (1997). Do extracurricular activities protect against early school dropout? Developmental Psychology, 33(2), 241-253. doi:10.1037/0012-1649.33.2.241
design: Longitudinal correlational study (annual assessments grade 7 to 12; person-oriented cluster analysis)
population_location: 392 adolescents (206 girls, 186 boys); authors at UNC Chapel Hill, US (site not named in abstract)
outcome: Early school dropout (failure to complete grade 11)
effect_as_reported: Dropout rate among at-risk students markedly lower for prior extracurricular participants (p < .001); 16% dropped out overall. Middle school: only athletics differentiated dropouts; high school arts near-significant (p = .08)
excerpt: Findings indicate that the school dropout rate among at-risk students was markedly lower for students who had earlier participated in extracurricular activities compared with those who did not participate (p < .001).
note: ArtsEdSearch: "At the middle school level, it was only athletic participation that differentiated dropouts from non-dropouts; fine arts participation was not related to dropout". US location is inferred from the author affiliation.

population_location: Elementary and K-8 students in San Francisco USD and Oakland USD, California (2010-11 estimates, data 2009-10 to 2012-13)
outcome: Student attendance rate

excerpt: for students who were chronically absent in the prior year, Playworks was associated with slightly larger increases in attendance, 0.4 percent rather than 0.2 percent,
